# One Key Starts, Two Others Don't

A single key failing to engage a starter motor while others function normally is a classic automotive logic puzzle. In your specific scenario with the 2002 Hyundai Santa Fe, the symptoms point away from a simple mechanical failure in the starter or solenoid and toward an electrical gating mechanism within the ignition system itself. You have effectively isolated the fault by confirming that battery voltage, fuses, and the starter motor are functional; the issue occurs exclusively when the key is inserted and turned, regardless of whether it is your wife's original key or a spare copy.

The most common misconception in these scenarios is that a key is physically "worn down." While mechanical wear on the tumblers inside the cylinder can prevent the lock from turning, it rarely prevents the ignition switch contacts from closing if the key rotates fully. Since you have confirmed the key turns fine and all electrical accessories (lights, radio, dashboard) remain powered, the anti-theft security circuit is likely not cutting power to the entire vehicle's electronics. Instead, the starter solenoid requires a specific ground path or a dedicated ignition signal that is being interrupted only by the failing keys.

In legacy systems like the 2002 Santa Fe, the ignition switch contains internal contacts that act as switches for different circuits depending on the key position (ACC, ON, START). These contacts are often made of copper or brass and can develop a high-resistance layer due to oxidation or corrosion, even if the plastic housing looks pristine. When your wife inserts her key, the mechanical tumblers align and turn, but perhaps not with the precise torque or rotational smoothness required to fully depress the internal micro-switches that complete the starter circuit.

This explains why both keys behave identically. If the issue were purely physical wear on the key blade itself, a spare copy would likely work if it was cut slightly differently or if the user applied different insertion force. However, since both keys fail identically and your original key works perfectly, the variable is almost certainly the ignition switch assembly's sensitivity to the specific actuation profile of those two keys versus your original.

The fact that these are non-transponder keys (no rubber head) rules out the modern immobilizer system where the car refuses to crank because it cannot read a radio frequency chip. You mentioned the factory anti-theft system is dormant; this confirms we are dealing with a purely electromechanical issue. The starter solenoid engages only when the ignition switch sends a specific signal, which is likely being dropped or degraded by a corroded contact point in the "START" position.

The solution involves inspecting the ignition cylinder and switch assembly for internal corrosion. Sometimes, applying a high-quality electrical contact cleaner (not penetrating oil, which can attract debris) to the internal contacts of the ignition switch while turning the key can restore conductivity. However, given that this is an intermittent issue triggered specifically by two keys, the internal contacts may be pitted or oxidized beyond cleaning. Replacing the entire ignition lock cylinder assembly is often the most reliable fix, as it ensures a fresh set of tumblers and contact points.

Before condemning the starter motor to scrap, remember that the starter itself is not at fault if it cranks with your original key. The problem is strictly in the logic gate between the key rotation and the solenoid engagement. If cleaning the contacts does not resolve the issue, swapping the ignition switch assembly is the definitive repair path.
